passages.title: Who Cares for the Carers?
paragraphs: At the end of a fourteen-hour shift in the emergency department of a provincial hospital in northeastern Thailand, nurse Pimchanok Saengthong often sits in her car for twenty minutes before she can face the drive home. "I am not sad, exactly," she says. "I am just empty." Her experience is far from unusual. Across the world, the people whose job is to look after others are finding it increasingly hard to look after themselves.

Surveys conducted since the COVID-19 pandemic paint a worrying picture. A 2023 study of almost 3,000 doctors and nurses in Southeast Asia found that around four in ten reported symptoms of burnout, a state of emotional exhaustion, detachment from patients and a reduced sense of accomplishment. Rates were highest among junior staff and those who regularly worked night shifts. Burnout is not merely a private misfortune, either: it has been linked to more medical errors, lower patient satisfaction and experienced staff leaving the profession altogether.

Researchers increasingly argue that the roots of the problem lie less in individual weakness than in the conditions of work. Chronic understaffing, long and unpredictable hours, and growing administrative workloads leave little time for recovery between shifts. Another factor, sometimes called "moral injury", arises when clinicians know what a patient needs but are prevented from providing it by shortages of beds, equipment or time. Unlike ordinary stress, which usually fades after a period of rest, moral injury can leave lasting feelings of guilt and betrayal.

For many years, the standard response of hospitals has been to offer resilience training: workshops on mindfulness, breathing techniques and time management. Such programmes can help, and many staff appreciate them. Critics, however, point out that they place the burden of change on the very people who are already overloaded. "Teaching a nurse to breathe more calmly does not fix a roster that has her working six nights in a row," says Dr. Anan Rattanakul, a psychiatrist who studies workplace health.

A small number of hospitals are now experimenting with organisational solutions instead. One hospital in central Thailand introduced protected break times, hired additional ward clerks to take over routine paperwork, and set up confidential peer-support groups led by trained colleagues. After eighteen months, the proportion of nurses who said they intended to leave their jobs fell from 31 percent to 19 percent. Staff also reported that simply knowing their managers were listening made a noticeable difference to morale.

None of these measures is expensive compared with the cost of recruiting and training replacements. Yet they require hospital leaders to see staff well-being not as a personal matter but as a question of patient safety. As Pimchanok puts it, "If you want us to care for patients, someone has to care for us first."

passages.title: The Paddy Field Problem
paragraphs: Rice is the staple food of more than half of the world's population, but the way it is usually grown carries a hidden climate cost. When paddy fields are kept continuously flooded, the waterlogged soil is starved of oxygen. In these conditions, microbes known as methanogens break down plant material and release methane, a greenhouse gas that traps roughly 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide over a twenty-year period. Rice cultivation is estimated to produce around a tenth of the methane emitted by human activities.

A growing body of research suggests that much of this methane could be avoided through a surprisingly simple change. Under a technique called alternate wetting and drying (AWD), farmers allow the water in their fields to drain away until it falls about 15 centimetres below the soil surface, and only then flood the field again. They monitor the level using a plastic tube with holes in its sides, pushed vertically into the ground. Because air reaches the soil during the dry spells, the methane-producing microbes become far less active.

Results from field trials have been encouraging. In a three-year study involving 120 farms in central Thailand, researchers found that fields managed with AWD released, on average, 45 percent less methane than conventionally flooded fields, while yields remained statistically unchanged. Farmers also used about a quarter less irrigation water, which lowered their pumping costs. "We expected some trade-off in productivity," admitted the study's lead author, Dr. Kanokwan Prasertsuk, an agricultural scientist. "We simply did not find one."

The technique is not without drawbacks, however. Drying the soil can increase emissions of nitrous oxide, another powerful greenhouse gas, although most studies find that this offsets only a small part of the methane savings. AWD also works poorly in fields that cannot be drained easily, and in places where individual farmers have no say over when water arrives, as is often the case in large shared irrigation schemes.

The greater obstacle, researchers say, is persuading farmers to change long-established habits. Many growers worry that letting fields dry will encourage weeds or damage the crop, and the savings on water mean little to farmers who pay a fixed fee regardless of how much they use. As a result, voluntary uptake has been slow. "Asking farmers to change their methods purely to help the climate is, frankly, unrealistic," Dr. Kanokwan said.

Several schemes are now testing ways to reward farmers for making the switch. Some offer payments for each tonne of emissions avoided, financed through carbon markets; others provide free training and water tubes, or link the technique to premium prices for "low-carbon rice". Early results suggest that such incentives can double adoption rates within two growing seasons. Whether they can be scaled up affordably remains an open question. For a crop eaten by billions of people every day, however, even modest progress could make a measurable difference to the climate.

passages.title: Connected, but Lonely?
paragraphs: Today's young adults are the most digitally connected generation in history. Many have hundreds of online "friends", exchange messages from the moment they wake up, and can see at a glance what classmates on the other side of the city, or the world, are doing. Yet surveys in several countries have found that young adults report feeling lonely more often than older people do. This apparent paradox has led researchers to ask whether social media is part of the problem.

Early studies seemed to offer a clear answer. The more time people spent on social media, the lonelier they tended to say they felt. A 2022 survey of 2,400 university students in Thailand and Malaysia, for instance, found that those who used social platforms for more than four hours a day were nearly twice as likely to describe themselves as lonely as those who used them for less than an hour. Such findings were widely reported as proof that social media "causes" loneliness.

However, a link between two things does not show that one causes the other. It is equally possible that people who already feel isolated turn to their phones for company, so that loneliness leads to heavy use rather than the other way round. Longitudinal studies, which follow the same individuals over several years, suggest that the relationship probably runs in both directions and is weaker than early headlines implied.

More recent research has therefore shifted attention from how much people use social media to how they use it. Psychologists distinguish between active use, such as messaging friends, commenting and sharing, and passive use, which involves scrolling through other people's posts without interacting. Passive use appears to be the more harmful of the two, partly because it encourages upward social comparison: viewers measure their ordinary lives against carefully edited images of other people's holidays, achievements and celebrations. Active use, by contrast, is generally associated with feeling closer to others, especially when it supports relationships that also exist offline.

"The platform is not the enemy," says Dr. Nattaya Boonsri, a psychologist who counsels university students in Bangkok. "What matters is whether the screen is a bridge to other people or a window you just stare through." She encourages students to notice how they feel after using an app, and to replace some of the time spent scrolling with arranging face-to-face meetings.

Universities are beginning to respond. Some now run campaigns promoting "phone-free" social events, while others train student counsellors to ask about online habits during routine appointments. Experts warn, however, that such efforts are unlikely to succeed if they simply tell young people to log off. A more realistic goal is to help young adults use the technology in ways that strengthen, rather than replace, their real-world relationships.

passages.title: Understanding Vaccine Hesitancy: Causes, Contexts and Interventions
paragraphs: Vaccines are among the most cost-effective tools in public health, preventing millions of deaths every year from diseases such as measles, diphtheria and whooping cough. Their success, however, depends not only on scientific development and reliable supply but also on people's willingness to accept them. Over the past two decades, public health experts have become increasingly concerned about vaccine hesitancy, usually understood as a delay in accepting, or a refusal of, recommended vaccines even when they are readily available. Importantly, hesitancy is not the same as outright opposition. It describes a continuum that ranges from people who accept every vaccine but with some anxiety, through those who delay or accept only certain vaccines, to a small minority who refuse all of them.

Hesitancy is not a new phenomenon. In nineteenth-century England, resistance to smallpox vaccination was widespread, and opponents objected both to the procedure itself and to laws that made it compulsory. More recently, a now-retracted 1998 study that claimed a link between the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine and autism led to falling vaccination rates in several countries, followed by outbreaks of measles. What has changed is the speed at which doubts can spread. Social media allows misleading claims to reach millions of people within hours, often faster than health authorities are able to respond.

Researchers have proposed several frameworks to explain why people hesitate. One widely used model groups the causes into three categories, often referred to as the "3Cs". Confidence refers to trust in the safety and effectiveness of vaccines, in the health workers who deliver them and in the policymakers who decide which vaccines are needed. Complacency occurs when people perceive the risks of a disease as low, so that vaccination seems unnecessary. Convenience concerns practical barriers such as cost, distance, clinic opening hours and language. Later versions of the model have added further factors, including how far people search for and weigh up information themselves and their sense of collective responsibility.

An ironic consequence of successful vaccination programmes is that they can encourage complacency. When diseases such as polio or diphtheria are rarely seen, young parents may never have witnessed their effects and may come to fear the vaccine more than the illness. In this sense, vaccines can become "victims of their own success". A survey of 1,500 parents in three Southeast Asian countries found that those who could not name a single complication of measles were more than twice as likely to have delayed their child's vaccination as those who could name at least one.

Context also matters greatly. During the COVID-19 pandemic, studies in many countries found that hesitancy was shaped by political identity, previous experiences with the health system and levels of trust in government, not simply by knowledge about vaccines. In some communities, hesitancy reflected a history of injustice or discrimination in health care. For this reason, experts warn against treating hesitant individuals as merely ignorant. Labelling them in this way can deepen mistrust and push those with mild doubts towards firmer refusal.

What, then, works? Reviews of the evidence suggest that simply presenting people with more facts is often ineffective and may even backfire if it appears to dismiss their concerns. More promising are approaches that combine clear information with respectful dialogue. One technique, known as motivational interviewing, trains health workers to ask open questions, listen to patients' worries without judgement and help them reach their own decisions rather than lecturing them. In a trial at maternity clinics in northern Thailand, 87 percent of mothers whose nurses had received this training completed their infants' first-year vaccinations, compared with 76 percent in a comparison group.

Structural interventions can be equally important, particularly where convenience is the main barrier. Reminder messages sent by text or telephone, extended clinic hours and mobile teams that vaccinate people at workplaces, markets and schools have all been shown to raise coverage. In Thailand, village health volunteers have long helped to trace children who miss scheduled doses and to encourage their families to return. Because these volunteers live in the communities they serve, they are often trusted more than distant officials.

In short, vaccine hesitancy is a complex and context-specific phenomenon rather than a single problem with a single solution. Effective responses begin by identifying which concerns matter most in a particular community, whether they relate to confidence, complacency or convenience, and then selecting interventions accordingly. As misinformation continues to spread through digital channels, building and maintaining public trust is likely to remain the central challenge for immunisation programmes in the years ahead.

passages.title: Nicotine in the Pencil Case
paragraphs: Teachers in several provinces of northeastern Thailand say they are confiscating more electronic cigarettes from pupils than ever before, despite a national ban on the import and sale of the devices. A survey of 4,000 secondary school students in the region, carried out last year by university researchers, found that 17 percent of those aged 13 to 15 had tried vaping, up from 9 percent three years earlier.

Many of the devices seized look nothing like cigarettes. Shaped like highlighter pens, lipsticks or cartoon characters, they can easily be hidden in a pencil case. Most are bought online or through social media accounts and come in sweet flavours such as mango, bubble gum and milk tea, which health experts say are designed to appeal to young users.

Doctors warn that the products are far from harmless. Most contain nicotine, which is highly addictive and can affect the developing adolescent brain, harming attention, learning and memory. "Many students honestly believe they are inhaling flavoured water vapour," said Dr. Wilaiwan Somsri, a paediatrician at a provincial hospital. "By the time they discover it contains nicotine, they are already dependent."

In response, education officials plan to train at least one teacher in every secondary school in the region to lead lessons on the risks of vaping, and to work with police to target online sellers. Some parents, however, doubt that schools can solve the problem alone. "These things are delivered straight to our homes," said one mother in Udon Thani. "Enforcement has to start with the sellers, not the children."

passages.title: A New Kind of Farmhand
paragraphs: In the rice fields of Suphan Buri, the familiar sight of farmers carrying heavy tanks of chemicals on their backs is giving way to a new one: small drones flying a few metres above the crops, spraying fertiliser and pesticide in neat lines. Once a novelty, agricultural drones have spread rapidly across central and northeastern Thailand over the past five years.

Most farmers do not own the machines. Instead, they hire local operators, many of them young people who have returned from jobs in the city, who typically charge 60 to 80 baht per rai. A drone can treat a ten-rai field in under half an hour, a job that would take a worker most of a day by hand.

Supporters say the benefits go beyond speed. Because farmers no longer walk through the fields with sprayers, they are less exposed to harmful chemicals. Some newer models also use cameras and artificial intelligence to identify patches affected by pests or disease, so that chemicals are applied only where necessary. In a trial run by researchers at a northeastern university, this "targeted spraying" reduced pesticide use by about 30 percent.

The technology is not without risks. Spray can drift onto neighbouring fields, homes or ponds when drones are flown in strong wind, and many operators have had little formal training. Owners must register their drones with the authorities, but experts say the rules on agricultural spraying need to be clearer. "The drone is only a tool," said Somchai Intharawong, a Chai Nat farmer who now runs a spraying business. "How safely it is used depends on the person holding the controller."

passages.title: Micro-credentials and Lifelong Learning in a Changing Labour Market
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, education was widely regarded as something completed early in life. A person studied at school and perhaps at university, obtained a qualification, and then relied on that qualification for the rest of a working career. This model is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain. Rapid technological change, the automation of routine tasks and longer working lives mean that many adults will need to update their skills several times. Governments and universities have therefore placed growing emphasis on lifelong learning, and one of the most widely discussed tools for achieving it is the micro-credential.

Although definitions vary, a micro-credential is generally understood as a record of learning achieved through a short, focused course, typically lasting from a few hours to several weeks. Whereas a degree covers a broad field of study, a micro-credential certifies a specific skill or competence, such as data visualisation, infection control or online teaching. Many are issued as digital badges, which contain information about what the learner did, how the learning was assessed and which institution awarded it. These can be shared on professional networking sites or attached to job applications.

Advocates argue that micro-credentials offer several advantages over traditional programmes. Because they are short and often delivered online, they allow working adults to study without leaving their jobs or paying the full fees of a degree. They also enable providers to respond quickly to changes in the labour market: a new course can be designed and launched within months, whereas the approval of a new degree programme may take several years. In addition, some micro-credentials are "stackable", meaning that several of them can be combined and counted towards a larger qualification, such as a diploma or a master's degree.

In Thailand, interest in this form of learning has grown alongside the development of credit bank systems, which allow learners to accumulate credits from different courses and institutions over time. A number of Thai universities now offer short certified courses in fields such as digital marketing, elderly care and artificial intelligence, some of which can later be transferred into degree programmes. A 2024 survey of 900 working adults in Bangkok and Khon Kaen found that 62 percent would consider taking a micro-credential within the next two years, with career advancement the reason most commonly given. Supporters argue that such arrangements could be especially useful in a rapidly ageing society, where many people will need to work for longer and may change careers more than once.

Despite this enthusiasm, critics have raised several concerns. The first is quality. Because micro-credentials can be offered by universities, private companies, professional bodies and online platforms, the standards behind them vary considerably. Some micro-credentials involve rigorous assessment, while others certify little more than attendance. Without consistent quality assurance, learners may find it difficult to judge which courses are worth their time and money, and employers may struggle to interpret what a particular badge actually represents.

A second concern relates to recognition. A micro-credential is valuable only if others accept it as evidence of competence. Surveys of employers have produced mixed results: many say they value specific, up-to-date skills, yet relatively few report having used micro-credentials when making hiring decisions. In one study of 300 human resources managers in Southeast Asia, fewer than a quarter could correctly explain what a micro-credential was. This suggests that the currency of these credentials in the job market remains limited, at least for the time being.

Equity is a third issue. Micro-credentials are often promoted as a way of widening access to education, yet evidence suggests that they are taken up most often by people who already hold degrees. Learners with lower levels of education, limited internet access or little free time may benefit least, even though such workers are often the most vulnerable to automation. Older employees in rural areas, for example, may lack both the digital skills and the reliable connections needed to complete courses online. If this pattern continues, micro-credentials could widen rather than narrow existing inequalities.

None of these problems means that micro-credentials should be abandoned. Rather, they point to the need for national frameworks that set common standards, describe learning outcomes clearly and link short courses to recognised qualifications. Several countries are developing such frameworks, often in partnership with employers. Targeted financial support, such as government-funded learning accounts, may also help to reach adults who would otherwise be left behind. If these conditions are met, micro-credentials could become a valuable part of a genuinely lifelong education system rather than simply a fashionable label.

passages.title: The Sound of Traffic
paragraphs: Long-term exposure to traffic noise may raise the risk of high blood pressure, even among people who say they have grown used to it, according to a new study of residents in three Southeast Asian capital cities. Researchers followed 5,200 adults for six years, using detailed noise maps to estimate the average sound level outside each participant's home.

Participants living where night-time road noise regularly exceeded 55 decibels were 18 percent more likely to develop hypertension during the study than those on quieter streets, after differences in age, income, smoking and air pollution had been taken into account. The link was strongest among people whose bedrooms faced the road.

The findings add to a growing body of evidence that noise is more than a nuisance. Sudden loud sounds trigger the body's stress response, releasing hormones such as cortisol and adrenaline, which raise heart rate and blood pressure. Crucially, this happens even during sleep, so people may be affected without waking up or remembering being disturbed.

"Many residents told us the traffic no longer bothered them," said the study's lead author, Dr. Thanakorn Wongsuwan, an environmental epidemiologist. "But their bodies were still reacting." He argues that cities should treat noise as a public health issue, using measures such as quieter road surfaces, lower night-time speed limits and stricter controls on modified motorcycle exhausts. Residents, he added, can reduce their own exposure by sleeping in rooms away from the street where possible.

passages.title: A Hard Summer Underwater
paragraphs: Marine scientists are reporting widespread coral bleaching along the coasts of southern Thailand after sea temperatures remained unusually high for much of the hot season. Surveys of more than 40 reef sites in the Andaman Sea and the Gulf of Thailand found that over half of the corals examined had turned partly or completely white.

Bleaching occurs when corals are stressed by heat. Normally, tiny algae living inside coral tissue supply the coral with most of its food through photosynthesis and give it its colour. When the water stays too warm for several weeks, the corals expel these algae, leaving their white skeletons visible through transparent tissue. Bleached corals are not yet dead, but if high temperatures persist, many will starve.

"We have seen bleaching before, but never this widespread or this early in the year," said Dr. Chalida Thongkham, a marine biologist who led one of the survey teams. She noted that reefs which had recovered from earlier events had not had enough time to regain their full strength before the latest heatwave struck.

In response, authorities have temporarily closed several popular dive sites to reduce additional pressure from tourism, and volunteers have been asked to report bleaching through a mobile app. Scientists stress that local measures, such as limiting pollution and protecting the fish that keep seaweed under control, can help reefs recover. In the long term, however, they warn that the survival of coral reefs will depend on global efforts to slow the warming of the oceans.

passages.title: Robotics and the Care of Older People in Ageing Societies
paragraphs: Populations across East and Southeast Asia are ageing at an unprecedented pace. In Japan, almost three in ten people are now aged 65 or over, while in Thailand around one in five citizens has passed the age of 60, making it one of the most rapidly ageing countries in the developing world. As the number of older people grows, the number of working-age adults available to care for them is shrinking. Falling birth rates, the migration of young people to cities and the increasing participation of women in paid work have all weakened the family-based care on which many societies have traditionally relied.

Against this background, governments, technology companies and researchers have turned to robotics as a possible partial solution. The robots being developed for elderly care fall broadly into three groups. Assistive robots help with physical tasks, such as lifting a person from a bed into a wheelchair or supporting someone as they walk. Monitoring robots and sensors track vital signs, detect falls and remind users to take their medication. Social robots, finally, are designed to provide companionship and mental stimulation through conversation, games or simple emotional responses.

Of these, social robots have attracted the most public attention. Some resemble animals such as seals or puppies and respond to touch and voice with movements and sounds. Studies in nursing homes have reported that interacting with such robots can reduce agitation and improve mood among residents with dementia, producing effects similar to those of animal-assisted therapy but without the need to look after a live animal. However, many of these studies have been small, short and conducted without control groups, so their conclusions should be treated with caution.

Assistive and monitoring technologies may offer more measurable benefits. Lifting and moving patients is a leading cause of back injuries among care workers, and robotic lifting devices can reduce this risk. Fall-detection systems can alert staff within seconds, shortening the time an older person may lie on the floor before help arrives. In a pilot project at a long-term care facility in northern Thailand, the introduction of bed sensors and a robotic transfer aid was associated with a 40 percent reduction in the time staff spent on routine night-time checks, allowing nurses to concentrate on residents who needed direct attention.

Despite these potential advantages, the adoption of care robots has been slower than many predicted. Cost is one obstacle: advanced robots remain expensive to buy and maintain, which puts them beyond the reach of most care homes and families in middle-income countries. Usability is another. Devices designed in laboratories often perform poorly in crowded, unpredictable real-world settings, and older users with limited eyesight, hearing or experience of technology may find such machines confusing. Care staff, too, may resist technologies that they feel have been introduced without consultation or that add to their workload.

The use of robots in care also raises ethical questions. Critics worry that robots could be used to justify cuts in human staff, leaving older people more isolated rather than less. Others question whether it is acceptable to give a person with dementia a robotic pet that he or she may believe to be alive, arguing that this involves a form of deception. Monitoring technologies, meanwhile, collect large amounts of personal data, raising concerns about privacy and about who controls information on residents' health and daily routines.

Researchers who study care robots increasingly argue that the central question is not whether machines can replace human caregivers but how they can best support them. Care involves not only completing tasks but also recognising and responding to a person's feelings and preferences, abilities that current machines do not possess. A robot can lift a patient, but it cannot sense that she is frightened or lonely. From this perspective, the most promising role for robots is to take over physically demanding or repetitive work, freeing human carers to spend more time on the relational aspects of care that matter most to older people.

For countries such as Thailand, where long-term care systems are still being developed, this suggests a cautious and practical approach. Rather than investing heavily in expensive humanoid machines, policymakers might prioritise affordable technologies with clear benefits, such as fall sensors and lifting aids, and evaluate them carefully in local settings. Equally important will be involving older people, families and care workers in decisions about which technologies to adopt and how. Robots may well become a valuable part of elderly care, but only if they are designed and deployed around human needs.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Robots offer real but limited benefits in elderly care and need careful use.
Social robots have now been proven to cure agitation in people living with dementia.
Robots will soon take over most caring work in Asia's rapidly ageing societies.
High costs mean that care robots have no future in middle-income countries.
questions.explain: บทความชี้ประโยชน์ (¶3–4) อุปสรรคและประเด็นจริยธรรม (¶5–6) แล้วสรุปใน ¶8 ว่าหุ่นยนต์จะมีคุณค่า "only if they are designed and deployed around human needs" ตัวเลือก B ผิดเพราะ ¶3 เตือนว่าผลการศึกษา "should be treated with caution" และ D เกินจริงเพราะ ¶8 ยังแนะนำเทคโนโลยีราคาไม่แพง

questions.q: In which country are almost three in ten people aged 65 or over? (Answer in ONE WORD from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶1: "In Japan, almost three in ten people are now aged 65 or over" อย่าตอบ Thailand ซึ่งตัวเลขคือราวหนึ่งในห้าคนที่อายุเกิน 60 ปี

questions.q: The word 'unprecedented' in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to
options: steady and predictable
slow and gradual
never seen before
officially recorded
questions.explain: ¶1: "ageing at an unprecedented pace" หมายถึงความเร็วที่ไม่เคยเกิดขึ้นมาก่อน ซึ่งประโยคต่อมายืนยันด้วยคำว่า "most rapidly ageing" ตัวเลือก B ตรงข้ามกับบริบทเรื่องความรวดเร็ว

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in paragraph 1 as weakening family-based care?
options: Lower birth rates
Rising rents in cities
Young people moving to cities
More women in paid employment
questions.explain: ¶1 ระบุ "Falling birth rates, the migration of young people to cities and the increasing participation of women in paid work" ไม่มีเรื่องค่าเช่าที่อยู่อาศัย ตัวเลือก B เป็นกับดักเพราะมีคำว่า cities เหมือนข้อ C

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, which of the following is a function of monitoring robots?
options: Lifting people from beds into wheelchairs
Playing games and holding conversations
Helping older people walk more safely
Reminding users to take their medicine
questions.explain: ¶2: "Monitoring robots and sensors track vital signs, detect falls and remind users to take their medication" ตัวเลือก A และ C เป็นหน้าที่ของ assistive robots ส่วน B เป็นหน้าที่ของ social robots

questions.q: Interacting with robotic animals has produced effects similar to those of what kind of therapy? (Answer in NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶3: "producing effects similar to those of animal-assisted therapy but without the need to look after a live animal" คำว่า animal-assisted ที่มีขีดกลางนับเป็นหนึ่งคำ

questions.q: Why does the author point out that many studies of robotic companions were small, short and lacked control groups?
options: To indicate that their reported benefits are not yet firmly proven
To argue that robotic animals should be removed from nursing homes
To show that live animals are more effective than robots
To explain why dementia is difficult to study scientifically
questions.explain: ¶3 สรุปข้อจำกัดนี้ว่า "so their conclusions should be treated with caution" จึงเป็นการบอกว่าประโยชน์ยังไม่ได้รับการพิสูจน์อย่างหนักแน่น ตัวเลือก B เกินเลย เพราะผู้เขียนเพียงให้ระวังการสรุป ไม่ได้เสนอให้เลิกใช้

questions.q: According to paragraph 4, lifting and moving patients is a leading cause of what kind of injury among care workers? (Answer in NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶4: "Lifting and moving patients is a leading cause of back injuries among care workers" ซึ่งเป็นเหตุผลที่อุปกรณ์ยกด้วยหุ่นยนต์ช่วยลดความเสี่ยงได้

questions.q: According to paragraph 4, the pilot project in northern Thailand
options: cut the number of falls among residents by 40 percent
replaced night-shift nurses with robotic transfer aids
reduced the time staff spent on routine checks at night
was carried out in the emergency ward of a city hospital
questions.explain: ¶4: "a 40 percent reduction in the time staff spent on routine night-time checks" ตัวเลือก A ใช้ตัวเลข 40 ผิดสิ่ง เพราะสิ่งที่ลดลงคือเวลาตรวจตอนกลางคืน ไม่ใช่จำนวนการหกล้ม และ B ขัดกับข้อความที่ว่าพยาบาลได้ "concentrate on residents"

questions.q: Apart from cost, what other obstacle to the adoption of care robots is named in paragraph 5? (Answer in ONE WORD from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶5: "Cost is one obstacle... Usability is another" โครงสร้าง one... another บอกว่าเป็นอุปสรรคข้อที่สองต่อจากค่าใช้จ่าย

questions.q: It can be inferred from paragraph 5 that care robots would be more readily accepted by staff if
options: they were designed to look more like humans
they were tested only in laboratory conditions
they replaced the most experienced care workers
staff were consulted before their introduction
questions.explain: ¶5: เจ้าหน้าที่อาจต่อต้านเทคโนโลยี "that they feel have been introduced without consultation" จึงอนุมานได้ว่าการปรึกษาก่อนจะช่วยให้ยอมรับมากขึ้น ตัวเลือก B ขัดกับข้อความที่ว่าอุปกรณ์จากห้องทดลอง "often perform poorly" ในสถานการณ์จริง

questions.q: The word 'deception' in paragraph 6 is closest in meaning to
options: causing physical harm
misleading someone
ignoring someone's needs
treating someone unfairly
questions.explain: ¶6: การให้หุ่นยนต์สัตว์เลี้ยงแก่ผู้ป่วยสมองเสื่อม "that he or she may believe to be alive" ถูกมองว่าเป็น deception คือการทำให้เข้าใจผิด ตัวเลือก C เกี่ยวกับความกังวลเรื่องการลดพนักงานในประโยคก่อนหน้า ไม่ใช่ความหมายของคำนี้

questions.q: Besides who controls information, what concern do monitoring technologies raise because they collect personal data? (Answer in ONE WORD from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶6: "collect large amounts of personal data, raising concerns about privacy and about who controls information" คำตอบคือความเป็นส่วนตัว ไม่ใช่ deception ซึ่งเป็นประเด็นเรื่องหุ่นยนต์สัตว์เลี้ยง

questions.q: What does 'them' in paragraph 7 refer to?
options: human caregivers
care robots
older people
researchers who study robots
questions.explain: ¶7: "not whether machines can replace human caregivers but how they can best support them" they คือ machines ที่เป็นผู้สนับสนุน ส่วน them คือผู้ดูแลที่เป็นมนุษย์ ตัวเลือก B สลับบทบาทระหว่าง they กับ them

questions.q: What is the main purpose of paragraph 8?
options: To describe the history of long-term care in Thailand
To argue that humanoid robots are the best investment
To summarise the ethical objections to care robots
To apply the article's main conclusions to Thailand
questions.explain: ¶8 เริ่มด้วย "For countries such as Thailand... this suggests a cautious and practical approach" คือนำข้อสรุปของบทความมาใช้กับบริบทไทย ตัวเลือก B ตรงข้ามกับคำแนะนำ "Rather than investing heavily in expensive humanoid machines"

passages.title: Turning the Page Together
paragraphs: Every Tuesday morning, about twenty retired residents gather at a small community library in Khon Kaen to read aloud, discuss short stories and swap books. What began two years ago as a simple social activity has now attracted the attention of researchers, who believe the club may be doing more than helping its members pass the time.

A team of public health researchers compared 64 club members aged 60 to 82 with a similar group of older adults who did not attend. After six months, the members performed better on tests of short-term memory and reported fewer symptoms of low mood. Those who came to at least three sessions a month showed the greatest improvements.

Organisers believe that the combination of mental challenge and friendship is the key. "Reading keeps the brain working, but talking about a story with others is what brings people back each week," said Malee Chaiyasit, a retired teacher who founded the club. Several members said the meetings had given them a reason to leave the house and a new circle of friends.

The researchers point out that the study was small and that people who join such clubs may already be healthier or more active than others. Even so, they describe the results as encouraging, especially because reading groups are cheap and easy to organise. The library now plans to start a second group in the afternoons, and staff have begun recording audiobooks for members with poor eyesight.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Older adults in Khon Kaen now prefer audiobooks to printed books.
Retired teachers score higher on memory tests than other older people.
Reading alone helps memory more than discussing books with other people.
A reading club for older people seems to benefit their memory and mood.
questions.explain: ¶2 รายงานว่าสมาชิก "performed better on tests of short-term memory and reported fewer symptoms of low mood" และย่อหน้าอื่นขยายความเรื่องชมรมนี้ ตัวเลือก C ขัดกับ ¶3 ที่ว่าการพูดคุยกับผู้อื่นคือสิ่งที่ทำให้คนกลับมา

questions.q: The word 'swap' in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to
options: borrow
exchange
review
recommend
questions.explain: ¶1: สมาชิก "read aloud, discuss short stories and swap books" คือแลกหนังสือกัน ตัวเลือก A ใกล้เคียงแต่ borrow คือยืมจากผู้อื่นฝ่ายเดียว ส่วน swap คือการให้และรับแลกกัน

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, which club members showed the greatest improvements?
options: Those who attended at least three sessions a month
Those who were aged between 60 and 82
Those who had worked as school teachers before retiring
Those who had joined the club two years earlier
questions.explain: ¶2: "Those who came to at least three sessions a month showed the greatest improvements" ตัวเลือก B ผิดเพราะช่วงอายุ 60–82 ปีคือสมาชิกทุกคนในการศึกษา ไม่ใช่กลุ่มที่ดีขึ้นมากที่สุด

questions.q: What does 'them' in paragraph 3 refer to?
options: the organisers
the stories
several members
other library users
questions.explain: ¶3: "Several members said the meetings had given them a reason to leave the house" ผู้ที่ได้เหตุผลให้ออกจากบ้านคือสมาชิกที่ให้สัมภาษณ์ ตัวเลือก A ผิดเพราะผู้จัดเป็นผู้ให้ความเห็นในประโยคก่อนหน้า ไม่ใช่ผู้กล่าวประโยคนี้

questions.q: According to paragraph 4, what does the library plan to do next?
options: Close the morning group and move it to the afternoon
Open a second group that will meet in the afternoons
Train volunteers to test members' memory each month
Buy large-print books for members with poor eyesight
questions.explain: ¶4: "The library now plans to start a second group in the afternoons" ตัวเลือก D เป็นกับดัก เพราะสำหรับผู้มีปัญหาสายตา เจ้าหน้าที่อัดหนังสือเสียง (audiobooks) ไม่ใช่ซื้อหนังสือตัวพิมพ์ใหญ่ และ A ผิดเพราะกลุ่มใหม่เป็นกลุ่มที่สอง ไม่ได้ย้ายกลุ่มเดิม

questions.q: It can be inferred from paragraph 4 that the researchers
options: think larger studies are needed to confirm the results
believe club members were less healthy at the start
plan to close the club once the study has finished
consider reading groups too costly for most communities
questions.explain: ¶4: นักวิจัยยอมรับว่า "the study was small" และผู้เข้าร่วมอาจสุขภาพดีอยู่แล้ว จึงอนุมานได้ว่าต้องการการศึกษาที่ใหญ่ขึ้นเพื่อยืนยันผล ตัวเลือก B ตรงข้ามกับข้อความที่ว่าสมาชิก "may already be healthier" และ D ขัดกับ "cheap and easy to organise"
